prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I teach my friend, a fisherman gone blind, to cast true left, right or center and how far between lily pads and the fallen cedar. Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last? Our bait, worms, have no professors, they live in darkness, can be taught fear of light. Cut into threes even sixes they live separate lives, recoil from light. He tells me, “I am seldom blind when I dream, morning is anthracite, I play blind man’s bluff, I cannot find myself, my shoe, the sink, tell time, but that’s spilled milk and ink, the lost and found I cannot find. I can tell the difference between a mollusk and a whelk, a grieving liar and a lemon rind.” Laughing, he says, “I still hope the worm will turn,pink, lank, and warm, dined out on apples of good fortune. Books have a faintly legible smell. Divorced from the sun, I am a kind of bachelor henpecked by the night. Sometimes I use my darkness well— in the overcast and sunlight of my mind. I can still wink, sing, my eyes are songs.” Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last? He could not fish, he could not walk, he fell in his own feces. He wept. He died where he fell.The power of beauty to right all wrongs is hard for me to sell.

Keywords: Darkness, Our, Cut

outputs.L1:
I teach my friend, a fisherman gone blind, to cast true—left, right, or center—and to judge the distance between the lily pads and the fallen cedar. Darkness is precious; how long will darkness last?

Our bait—the worms—have no professors. They live in darkness and can be taught to fear the light. Cut into thirds, even sixths, they live separate lives, recoiling from the light.

He tells me, “I am seldom blind when I dream. Morning is anthracite. I play blind man’s bluff: I cannot find myself, my shoe, the sink; I cannot tell time. But that is spilled milk and ink—the lost and found I cannot find. I can tell the difference between a mollusk and a whelk, a grieving liar and a lemon rind.”

Laughing, he says, “I still hope the worm will turn—pink, lank, and warm, having dined on apples of good fortune. Books have a faintly legible smell. Divorced from the sun, I am a kind of bachelor, henpecked by the night. Sometimes I use my darkness well—in the overcast and sunlight of my mind. I can still wink, sing; my eyes are songs.”

Darkness is precious; how long will darkness last?

He could not fish. He could not walk. He fell in his own feces. He wept. He died where he fell. The power of beauty to right all wrongs is hard for me to sell.
outputs.L2:
I instruct my friend, a fisherman who has lost his sight, in aiming his cast accurately—to the left, the right, or straight ahead—and in judging the distance between the water lilies and the toppled cedar tree. Darkness has value, but how much longer can it remain?

The worms we use for bait have no teachers. They inhabit darkness and can learn to dread illumination. Slice them into three parts, or even six, and each piece continues living on its own, shrinking away from light.

He tells me that in dreams he can usually see. On waking, everything is coal-black. He gropes about as though playing blindman’s buff, unable to locate himself, his shoe, or the sink, and unable to read the time. Yet he dismisses these losses as irreversible—like spilled milk or ink—and says that even the lost-and-found is beyond his finding. Still, he can distinguish a mollusk from a whelk, a deceitful mourner from the peel of a lemon.

With laughter, he says he continues to hope that fortune will change: that the worm will become rosy, slender, and warm after feasting on lucky apples. To him, books possess a barely decipherable scent. Separated from sunlight, he feels like an unmarried man constantly nagged by night. At times, however, he puts his blindness to good use within the shifting clouds and brightness of his imagination. He can still wink and sing; his eyes themselves are music.

Darkness matters, but how long can it endure?

Eventually he was unable to fish or even walk. He collapsed into his own excrement, cried, and died in the place where he had fallen. After that, I find it difficult to believe—or persuade anyone—that beauty has the power to set every injustice right.
outputs.L3:
The speaker teaches his blind fisherman friend to cast accurately by translating the visible world into precise spatial instructions. Through patient guidance—indicating direction, distance, and the position of the water—the speaker helps him compensate for what he cannot see. Fishing becomes an act of trust and cooperation, as the fisherman relies on voice, memory, bodily movement, and his awareness of the surrounding space.

The fisherman describes blindness as profoundly disorienting, yet he does not present it as a complete absence of perception. He remains sensitive to differences in sound, touch, movement, and degrees of darkness. He also retains an imaginative inner life filled with memories and visions. His experience therefore complicates the simple opposition between sight and blindness: although the external world has become difficult to navigate, his senses and imagination continue to give it shape and meaning.

Darkness is portrayed in equally contradictory terms. At times it seems precious, intimate, and fertile, creating a hidden world in which imagination can survive. At other times it is oppressive, isolating, and inescapable. This ambiguity connects the fisherman with the worms used as bait. Both inhabit darkness, but neither is protected by it. The worms are taken from the earth and exposed to suffering, while the fisherman is trapped within a condition that increasingly limits his freedom and independence.

Despite these hardships, the fisherman responds with humor, hope, and imaginative resilience. His wit allows him to preserve a sense of dignity, while fishing offers companionship and continued engagement with the world. Yet these qualities cannot halt his physical decline. As his condition worsens, he loses the independence he once maintained and eventually becomes helpless before dying.

The speaker ultimately refuses to turn this suffering into a comforting lesson. Friendship, imagination, and moments of beauty may offer temporary consolation, but they cannot undo the injustice of the fisherman’s fate. Beauty does not redeem his pain or make his death acceptable. The conclusion therefore remains deliberately unresolved and unsentimental, insisting that suffering must be recognized for what it is rather than transformed into an aesthetically pleasing source of meaning.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores blindness, friendship, and mortality through the relationship between its narrator and a blind fisherman. The narrator teaches the man how to cast, an activity that ordinarily depends on sight, accuracy, and an awareness of distance. For the fisherman, however, casting becomes an act of trust. He must rely on touch, sound, rhythm, and the narrator’s guidance as he attempts to participate in a world that has become increasingly inaccessible to him. Their shared activity briefly creates a sense of companionship and purpose, suggesting that friendship can help a person adapt to physical loss.

Yet the fisherman does not describe his blindness in purely sentimental terms. He uses dark humor to speak about his condition, turning fear and frustration into jokes that protect him from pity. His dreams and vivid sensory language also reveal the persistence of his imagination. Although his visible world has diminished, his inner life remains active, filled with remembered images, physical sensations, sounds, and desires. These details resist the idea that blindness has erased his identity. At the same time, they emphasize the painful contrast between the richness of what he can imagine and the limitations of what he can now experience.

Fishing therefore acquires a symbolic importance. Casting a line into unseen water resembles an attempt to reach beyond isolation and uncertainty. The fisherman cannot know exactly where the line will fall or what, if anything, it will bring back. In this sense, the act reflects the human need to hope despite incomplete knowledge and declining power. The narrator’s instruction may help him recover a temporary sense of competence, but it cannot restore his sight or remove the loneliness created by his condition.

As the fisherman’s health deteriorates, the poem’s tone becomes increasingly bleak. His decline exposes the limits of both humor and imagination. The strategies that once allowed him to endure his diminished world cannot prevent physical suffering or death. Likewise, the narrator’s companionship, though sincere, proves insufficient. Friendship can offer moments of dignity and connection, but it cannot permanently protect another person from illness, isolation, or mortality.

The fisherman’s lonely death gives the poem its final emotional force. It challenges any comforting belief that beauty, memory, or human closeness can fully redeem suffering. The lessons in casting and the moments of shared experience still matter, but they do not produce a miraculous transformation. Instead, they become fragile acts of care performed in the face of an irreversible loss.

Ultimately, the poem presents hope as necessary but limited. Imagination can enlarge a diminished world, humor can make pain briefly bearable, and companionship can interrupt loneliness. None of these, however, can defeat death or erase suffering. By refusing an easy consolation, the poem offers a sober meditation on the value and insufficiency of human connection: friendship cannot save the fisherman, but it can bear witness to his life and preserve the memory of his struggle.
outputs.L5:
Darkness gathered around us, thick and silent, swallowing every familiar shape. Our footsteps echoed through the empty street, the only proof that we were still moving.

Then a thin blade of morning cut across the horizon.

For a moment, the night resisted. But light entered through the smallest opening, and darkness—no matter how deep—could not remain whole.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about teaching a blind fisherman friend to cast between lily pads, using worms, dreams, darkness, wordplay, and a tragic ending that questions whether beauty can redeem suffering.
counterfactuals.output:
I taught my blind friend Elias to cast between the lily pads by naming the pond in distances: three breaths to the left, a heron’s cry beyond the reeds, the soft applause of frogs where the water opened. He listened with his whole body. “Sight is just one way of guessing,” he said, threading a worm onto the hook. The worm twisted like a small question mark, asking what earth had done to deserve the dark.

We practiced until his line could whisper through the narrow green corridors without bruising a single flower. Cast, I told him, and he laughed: “As in throw, or as in the characters trapped in a play?” Both, I said. Always both. The hook vanished with a kiss. Rings traveled outward, touching pad after pad, as if the pond were dreaming in braille.

Elias dreamed of fish before he caught them. Silver bodies swam through his sleep, each scale a tiny moon. He said darkness was not empty but crowded: with voices, warm rain, the remembered hands of his mother, the bright weight of things he had never seen. “Perhaps beauty is what darkness makes when it wants company,” he told me.

That autumn, on a cold morning when mist erased even my sight, his boot slipped from the bank. I heard the splash, the snapped reed, the reel still turning. I reached where his voice had been, but the pond had already closed over him, lily pads trembling like green hands unwilling to confess. We found his rod downstream. On the hook, the worm remained, alive and blind in its own small way.

Now I cast alone between the flowers. Every line I throw seems also a sentence, and every sentence ends where the water begins. At dusk the lilies open pale as promises, and I hate them for being beautiful. Then I love them, and hate myself for that.

If beauty cannot pull one drowning man from darkness, what does it redeem—suffering, or only those of us left on shore to name it?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental elegy for a fisherman who has gone blind. Include the recurring line “Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?” and end with the speaker doubting the power of beauty to right all wrongs.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Soundings for a Blind Fisherman**

At dawn he knots the sea by touch—  
hemp, hook, the cold arithmetic of bait.  
Gulls tear white holes in the air  
he cannot enter.

**Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?**

Once, the horizon obeyed him:  
a blue blade laid flat,  
a weather-script he read  
in the bruising of clouds.

Now wind is his compass.  
Salt, his small burning country.  
He hears the nets descend—

        down  
          through green  
            into no-color—

and each cork knocks the hull  
like a fist from beneath.

**Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?**

We mourn not the man, but the lantern  
extinguished behind his eyes;  
the silver schools that once turned  
all at once, one body,  
one thought flashing.

He says the sea has not vanished.  
It has moved inward.

There, waves break without light.  
There, his dead wife walks the shoal  
with her skirt gathered above her knees.  
There, every lost boat returns  
without its drowned.

**Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?**

He lifts his face. Evening  
presses its black coin into each socket.  
Someone describes the sunset—  
copper, violet, a wound rimmed with gold—  
and he laughs:

*Beauty is always arriving  
after it is needed.*

The tide keeps no elegy.  
It erases even its erasing.  
His hands, scarred and certain,  
draw the wet rope home.

Fish strike the deck like fallen stars.  
Their scales shine for everyone but him.

**Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?**

I want to call that shining mercy.  
I want the sea to mean forgiveness.  
But standing beside him in the beautiful, useless dusk,  
I doubt beauty has the power to right all wrongs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal, lyrical monologue in which a blind man jokes about dreams, lost objects, worms fearing light, books having a smell, and his eyes being songs, before the poem turns brutally toward his decline and death.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep my dreams in a cracked blue cup.  
They spill, naturally. Dreams are clumsy drinkers.  
Every morning I ask the floor,  
“Have you seen a small white horse?  
A staircase? My mother’s left hand?”  
The floor says nothing.  
Floors are famous liars.

I have lost many things:  
three buttons, seven summers,  
a brass key to a door that never existed.  
Once I lost the moon for a week.  
No one noticed.

The worms, I’m told, are afraid of light.  
Poor fools. Imagine fearing  
what you’ve never seen.  
I fear spoons, myself—  
their cold little faces,  
always pretending to know me.

Books announce themselves by scent:  
dust, rain, glue, another man’s fingers.  
A library is a forest after thunder.  
I open a book and the dead breathe out.  
Sometimes they cough.  
Sometimes they whisper,  
“Turn the page, blind brother.  
We cannot do it anymore.”

And my eyes?  
My eyes are songs with no mouths.  
One is a lullaby buried under snow.  
The other is a hymn  
a drunk angel forgot halfway through.  
If you put your ear to them,  
you may hear black violins,  
or the sea dragging its chains.

That was my joke.

Now the hands go first.  
They shake the cup empty.  
They cannot button the shirt,  
cannot find the spoon I feared,  
cannot wipe the spit from my chin.  
My legs become two wet ropes.  
My teeth loosen in their red rooms.  
The bed learns my weight  
and keeps it.

Soon I am all smell:  
medicine, urine, wool,  
the sweet rot of flowers  
brought by people who speak too brightly.  
They say I look peaceful.  
They lie worse than floors.

Inside me, something gnaws  
with patient white teeth.  
It eats the summers,  
the staircase, my mother’s hand.  
It eats the songs from my eyes.  
It eats my name until only a sound remains,  
then eats the sound.

At the end, I will open my mouth  
for one last joke—  
but death will put its fist inside  
and turn me off.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a literary prose-poem narrated by someone teaching a blind friend how to fish. Let the friend speak in playful paradoxes and puns, repeat a haunting question about darkness, then contrast the beauty of the language with an unsentimental account of his death.
counterfactuals.output:
I taught Elias to fish by putting the river into his hands.

First the rod: cork grip, reel seat, the small silver bail. Then the line, almost nothing between thumb and forefinger, a nerve extended into weather. I guided his hands through the cast—back, pause, forward—and the sinker struck the water with a sound like a coin dropped into a deep well.

“So,” he said, smiling toward the splash, “I throw away what I want returned.”

“That’s casting.”

“And if I catch nothing?”

“That’s fishing.”

He laughed. “A fine net of contradictions.”

We stood knee-deep in the current. The river pressed its cold argument around our boots. I described the morning badly: mist unbuttoning from the reeds, willows combing green hair over the bank, sunlight broken into scales.

Elias tilted his face toward the warmth. “Careful,” he said. “You’ll make the day too beautiful to touch.”

I showed him how to feel a bite: not the pull itself, but the hesitation before it, the quick syllable traveling up the line.

“Listen with your fingers,” I said.

“My fingers have ears,” he answered, “but they’re hard of herring.”

He waited, patient as a closed door. A kingfisher cracked blue across the river. I told him.

“Blue,” he said. “That loud color.”

Then, more quietly: “What color is the darkness when no one is looking?”

I said darkness had no color.

“Then it matches everything.”

His float dipped. He jerked too soon and reeled in an empty hook.

“I caught the one that got away,” he said. “It was enormous.”

By noon he could cast without me. The line hissed out over the water, invisible even to my eyes once it entered the glare. I told him the river was carrying the sky on its back.

“Poor river,” he said. “All that heaven and nowhere to set it down.”

A trout took the bait. The rod bowed. Elias stiffened, astonished by the living weight at the other end.

“Now?” he asked.

“Now.”

He reeled. The fish came flashing through the shallows, furious and beautiful, a wet blade hammered from moonlight. I cupped it while he touched its flank, its cold muscle, the frantic hinge of the gills.

“So this is silver,” he whispered.

“This is a trout.”

“Names, names. You sighted people are always throwing nets over things.”

We released it. For a moment it rested between our hands, then vanished with one stroke.

Elias listened to the water close.

“What color is the darkness when no one is looking?”

I gave him a different answer. I said perhaps darkness was the color left behind when everything else had gone.

He frowned. “That sounds expensive.”

Years later, in the hospital, there was no river. No mist lifted from reeds. No kingfisher split the air. A machine measured his heart in green angles. Cancer had entered his liver and lungs. Morphine dried his mouth. His abdomen filled with fluid. He vomited twice into a plastic basin. A nurse changed the sheets after he lost control of his bowels.

He did not become wise. He did not bless the room. He complained that the ice chips tasted of freezer and that dying was “a grave inconvenience.” Near dawn he asked for water, swallowed badly, and coughed until blood threaded the phlegm on his lip.

Then he said, “What color is the darkness when no one is looking?”

I held his hand. I did not answer.

At 6:17 his breathing stopped. His heart continued irregularly for less than a minute, then stopped too. The nurse checked his pupils, though he had never used them to see. She listened to his chest, noted the time, removed the oxygen tube, and pulled the sheet to his chin.

Nothing left his body that I could witness. No bird crossed the window. No hidden river spoke.

His hand cooled in mine, empty as a hook.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
